title: SIEVE is Simpler than LRU: an Efficient Turn-Key Eviction Algorithm for Web Caches
one_line: SIEVE is a cache eviction algorithm that adds a single tail-to-head 'hand' pointer to a FIFO queue with per-object visited bits, leaving retained objects in place, so it gets lazy promotion and quick demotion with less code and less metadata than LRU while beating 9 state-of-the-art policies on web-cache traces.

repo.evidence: Paper Availability section (p.13): 'The code and data used in this work are open-sourced at https://github.com/cacheMon/NSDI24-SIEVE. This repository includes both the simulator and prototypes.' fetch_result.json shows that exact URL was cloned; the org cacheMon is the authors' (contact sieve@cachemon.com, p.2 footnote).
repo.badge_evidence: none found - the USENIX NSDI'24 presentation page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch and no badge markers appear in repo/README.md or the repository tree; treat as unverified rather than confirmed absent

H1_open_repo.evidence: Official per paper Availability (p.13). The clone contains the real system, not a stub: libCacheSim/libCacheSim/cache/eviction/Sieve.c (287 lines; hand loop at :218-232), every Fig. 3 baseline (ARC.c, LIRS.c, TwoQ.c, Cacheus.c, Hyperbolic.c, Clock.c, WTinyLFU.c, LHD/lhd.cpp), the oracle variant belady/Sieve_Belady.c, and the CLI that emits the paper's miss ratios (bin/cachesim/main.c:62-69, cache_init.h:139-140). Apache-2.0, 87 stars. Caveat: the five production-library prototypes and the CacheLib throughput harness are external links (repo/README.md:63-67), not in this repo.

H2_no_root.evidence: CPU-only user-space simulator; no kernel module, eBPF, KVM, RDMA or /proc/sys write anywhere in the tree. All 'sudo' red-flag hits are in the optional convenience installer libCacheSim/scripts/install_dependency.sh (:4,:9,:28,:43,:55) and dead CI (libCacheSim/.travis.yml); glib/zstd/gperftools/xxhash/cmake are all conda-forge installable, and XGBoost/LightGBM are not needed because ENABLE_GLCACHE and ENABLE_LRB default OFF (CMakeLists.txt:23,26). CMakeLists.txt:20 mentions transparent_hugepage only in a comment; the actual code is an unprivileged madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) (dataStructure/hashtable/chainedHashTableV2.c:102) and -DUSE_HUGEPAGE=OFF removes it. libCacheSim/dockerfile is optional and replayable with conda. Single caveat: Fig. 11 (instructions/request, paper section 6.1) used 'perf stat', which is blocked on this machine (perf_event_paranoid=3) and must be substituted with user-space callgrind; it is not a headline result.

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: Single-node, CPU-only, no GPU and no network. The paper's own throughput evaluation used 1-16 threads (section 4.1, Fig. 6), matching this machine's 16 cores. Full-corpus simulation at paper scale exceeds 257 GB disk and 125 GB RAM (Table 1 implies ~4.7 TB for Twitter alone at 24 B/request, traceReader/customizedReader/oracle/oracleGeneralBin.h:24), but the CLI ships the exact scale-down levers needed: fractional cache sizes (bin/cachesim/cli_parser.c:426-451), --num-req cap (:140-142), and spatial object sampling (:304-307 -> traceReader/sampling/spatial.c:33), and traces are read zstd-compressed (CMakeLists.txt:150-162). The claim under test (relative ranking of eviction policies per trace) survives subsetting the trace corpus.

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: Dependencies are user-space installable: glib + argp + zstd required (CMakeLists.txt:141-162), tcmalloc optional (:169-177), ML deps gated off (:186-211); Python side is only numpy + matplotlib (scripts/plot_mrc_size.py:6-7). Data: five of the seven datasets are publicly downloadable and linked from the artifact (repo/README.md:52-58, ftp.pdl.cmu.edu/pub/datasets/twemcacheWorkload/cacheDatasets/ for tencentPhoto, wiki, twitter, metaKV, metaCDN) = 67 traces. CDN1 (1273 traces) and CDN2 (219) are proprietary (paper Table 1, p.6), but the public set itself contains three CDN object-cache datasets (Wiki CDN, Tencent Photo, Meta CDN) that cover the same regime, and Fig. 4 / Fig. 5 / Fig. 3c / Fig. 3f rest entirely on public traces. Recorded as a risk, not a fail.

reproduce.target: Figure 4a (p.7) plus the Meta KV / Meta CDN / Tencent / Wiki columns of Figure 5a, supporting the claim in section 4.2 that 'SIEVE outperforms all other algorithms on all four datasets at the large cache size' (13 traces, all public). Secondary: Fig. 3c (Twitter, 54 traces, large cache).
reproduce.scale_down: Use only the 13 public traces of Meta KV (5), Meta CDN (3), Wiki CDN (3) and Tencent Photo (2); skip the proprietary CDN1/CDN2 entirely. Keep every trace .zst-compressed on disk (default OPT_SUPPORT_ZSTD_TRACE, CMakeLists.txt:150-162) - ~120 GB instead of ~250 GB raw. Apply --sample-ratio 0.05 on Tencent (1038 M objects) and 0.01 on Twitter for the stretch target, validating the sampler first on Meta CDN where both sampled and unsampled runs are cheap. Run ONE algorithm at a time over both cache sizes (./cachesim TRACE oracleGeneral sieve 0.001,0.1 --ignore-obj-size 1 --num-thread 16) because bin/cachesim/main.c:35 instantiates n_algo x n_size live caches simultaneously and 11 x 2 on Tencent at 10% footprint would exhaust 125 GB. Use the paper's fractional sizes 0.001 and 0.1 directly (cli_parser.c:426-451). Skip --consider-obj-metadata (section 4.2 ignores object size anyway).
reproduce.effort: 4-6 person-days + ~200-400 CPU-core-hours (0 GPU-hours) + ~120 GB disk for compressed public traces
reproduce.rationale: Not H: (a) the documented install path is root-based apt + 'sudo make install' (scripts/install_dependency.sh) and must be re-derived under conda; (b) the scripts that actually draw the paper's figures are internal and broken - scripts/priv/plot/load_miss_ratio.py:15 imports a nonexistent module 'scripts.str_utils' (the file lives at scripts/utils/str_utils.py) and plot_mr_red_box.py:265-266 hardcodes /disk/cphy/result/ while plotting algorithms (S3FIFO_delay-0.1000-2-0.50) that appear in no paper figure - so per-trace aggregation must be rewritten (~80 lines against the stable output format at main.c:62-69); (c) two of seven datasets are proprietary and the public corpus needs subsetting plus sampling to fit disk and RAM. Not L: the algorithm, all ten baselines, B-LRU via --admission bloom-filter, the exact fractional-cache-size convention, the sampling lever, a working single-trace MRC script (scripts/plot_mrc_size.py), a synthetic Zipfian generator (scripts/data_gen.py) and a CTest suite all ship in-tree, the binary is a self-contained CLI, and there is no GPU, kernel, root or network dependency. No artifact badge evidence was found, so there is no 'Results Reproduced' signal to lean on.

addons.name: SIEVE-Ghost: scan resistance at a measured price
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that augmenting SIEVE with a small FIFO ghost queue of recently-evicted object IDs - readmitting a ghost-hit object with its visited bit already set so the hand skips it once - reduces miss ratio below both LRU and plain SIEVE on block/storage traces containing scan and loop patterns at small cache sizes (0.1-1% of footprint), while costing under 0.5 percentage points of miss ratio and under 10% of throughput on the web traces of Fig. 4.
addons.mechanism: Clone Sieve.c into Sieve_Ghost.c. Add a cache_t *ghost initialized via FIFO_init over IDs only, copying the pattern already debugged in S3FIFO.c:117-130; probe it in find() with ghost->remove(ghost, req->obj_id), which returns true on a ghost hit (S3FIFO.c:247-250); on a ghost hit set obj->sieve.freq = 1 instead of 0 in insert (Sieve.c:150) so the hand grants the object one free pass; push the victim's ID into the ghost just before cache_evict_base in Sieve_evict (Sieve.c:231). Register 'sieve-ghost' in cache_init.h beside 'sieve' (:139), declare the init in evictionAlgo.h (:166), and add the file to the eviction CMakeLists.txt. Sweep ghost size as a fraction of cache size to produce an efficiency-versus-metadata curve, reporting the cost in the paper's own currency (Table 3 lines-of-code and bytes-per-object). Include Marc Brooker's publicly-floated SIEVE-k (saturating counter) as a baseline rather than a contribution.
addons.motivating_evidence: Paper section 7.2 verbatim: 'SIEVE is not scan-resistant... Since SIEVE does not use a ghost cache - a shadow cache that keeps track of recently evicted items to make smarter future eviction decisions - it cannot recognize the popular objects when they are requested again. This problem is less severe on the large cache size, but when the cache size is small, we observe that having a ghost is critical to be scan-resistant. We conjecture that not being scan-resistant is probably the reason why SIEVE remained undiscovered over the decades.' The authors state both the diagnosis and the suspected cure and evaluate neither. The unresolved tension is that SIEVE's whole pitch is simplicity and zero parameters (section 4.4, Table 3), while a ghost adds metadata and a size knob - so a negative result is as informative as a positive one.
addons.feasibility_rationale: One new ~300-line file plus four registration lines; the ghost machinery already exists and is debugged two files away in S3FIFO.c. Evaluation reuses the existing cachesim CLI on MSR Cambridge / CloudPhysics / Alibaba-Tencent block traces, which are public and only single-digit GB, and the repo even ships a converter (scripts/priv/traceUtils/customized/msr_convert.py). CPU-only, no root, no new harness. Comfortably a 10-week job for 2-4 students.
addons.research_value_rationale: It attacks the paper's own named headline limitation and, if it works, promotes SIEVE from a web-cache algorithm to a general cache primitive - which an NSDI/FAST reviewer would care about. Marked down from H because the direction is anticipated by the paper itself and by ARC/LIRS/S3FIFO; a reviewer's first reaction is 'of course a ghost helps scans'. The value is in the quantification (how much ghost, at what metadata and throughput cost, and whether the web-workload win survives), not in the idea.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'SIEVE cache eviction scan resistance ghost cache extension 2025'; 'SIEVE-k OR scan-resistant SIEVE OR adaptive SIEVE follow-up'; 'libCacheSim SIEVE variant ghost queue block trace 2025'. Closest: Marc Brooker's blog https://brooker.co.za/blog/2023/12/15/sieve.html sketches SIEVE-k (a saturating k-bit counter instead of a single bit) as a scan-resistance idea - a blog post, not a paper, and a different mechanism from a ghost; https://www.isc.org/blogs/2025-sieve/ (2025) restates the operator-side scan-resistance concern. Upstream libCacheSim's develop branch still contains only a single Sieve.c with no ghost or SieveK variant (checked https://github.com/1a1a11a/libCacheSim/tree/develop/libCacheSim/cache/eviction). No peer-reviewed follow-up found. Rated partial because SIEVE-k is public, so it must be treated as a baseline.

addons.name: Adaptive hand floor for the small-cache regime
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that preventing SIEVE's hand from advancing into the newest f fraction of the queue, with f adapted online from the observed survival rate of newly inserted objects rather than fixed, reduces miss ratio at the 0.1%-of-footprint cache size on the public CDN and KV traces - closing SIEVE's gap to TwoQ and LHD - without regressing at the 10% cache size.
addons.mechanism: Sieve_evict (Sieve.c:218-232) walks obj->queue.prev until it finds freq == 0, wrapping only when it reaches the head (queue.prev == NULL). Add a hand-position counter and a floor: if the hand would come within f * n_obj of the head, wrap it to q_tail instead of continuing, so the freshest f of the queue is never an eviction candidate - SIEVE's structural analogue of TwoQ's fixed 25% reservation (TwoQ.c). The adaptive variant keeps two counters (objects examined in the head region versus objects retained there) and moves f by a multiplicative update, preserving the paper's zero-user-facing-parameter property. Register 'sieve-floor' in cache_init.h and evaluate at the paper's exact sizes 0.001 and 0.1 (cli_parser.c:426-451) against sieve, twoq, lhd and arc.
addons.motivating_evidence: Paper section 4.2: 'When the cache is very small, TwoQ and LHD sometimes outperform SIEVE... The primary reason for SIEVE's relatively poor performance is that new objects cannot demonstrate their popularity before being evicted when the cache size is very small... TwoQ does not suffer from the small cache sizes because it reserves a fixed 25% of the cache space for new objects, preventing overly aggressive demotion.' Visible in Fig. 3d-f (small-cache boxplots, where SIEVE is no longer the clear leader) and Fig. 5b (TwoQ wins both Meta datasets at the small cache size). Independently, section 5.3 / Fig. 9c shows the hand 'lingers at positions close to the head for most of the time', which is exactly the behaviour this add-on bounds.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Roughly 50-150 LOC confined to one function plus a registration line. The evaluation harness, cache sizes, baselines and traces are identical to the reproduction setup, so marginal compute cost is near zero. CPU-only, no root, no new data. Clearly doable by 2-4 students in 10 weeks, leaving room for the adaptive variant and an ablation against a fixed f.
addons.research_value_rationale: It targets the precise regime the paper concedes, and the adaptive formulation is a real design question rather than tuning: SIEVE's selling point is having no knobs, so only a self-tuning floor preserves the thesis. Marked down from H because a fixed reservation for new objects is well-trodden (TwoQ 1994, S3FIFO 2023) and a modest small-cache win would not surprise a reviewer; the surprising outcome would be a floor that also helps at large cache sizes.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'SIEVE cache small cache size limitation improve quick demotion reserve new objects follow-up 2025 2026'; 'SIEVE-k OR adaptive SIEVE'; 'arxiv 2025 cache eviction builds on SIEVE'. Results returned only the original paper, the authors' USENIX ;login: article, and popular-press coverage (techxplore, Emory News). The adaptive-parameter work that does exist attaches to other algorithms: SCION (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.01055) selects among six unmodified expert policies (SIEVE being one) via a workload fingerprint, and Learning-Augmented Heuristics / S4-FIFO (https://arxiv.org/html/2608.27975v1) adds tunable knobs to S3-FIFO, explicitly not to SIEVE. Nothing found that modifies SIEVE's hand movement.

addons.name: Closing the SIEVE-Belady gap with O(1) per-object state
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that a decision-maker using only O(1) per-object state available at eviction time (a 2-4 bit saturating access counter plus the object's insertion age in hand-revolutions) recovers at least 30% of the miss-ratio gap between SIEVE and the oracle SIEVE-Belady of Fig. 12c, on the public traces at both the 0.1% and 10% cache sizes, at under 10% added work per request.
addons.mechanism: belady/Sieve_Belady.c already implements the oracle rule of section 6.2 - reinsert the hand's candidate iff its next access is within C/mr. Step 1: build an instrumented variant that logs (access_count, insertion_age, queue_position, oracle_label) at every eviction decision. Step 2: fit a tiny offline model (decision stump / logistic regression / small lookup table, scikit-learn, CPU-seconds) on one dataset. Step 3: inline the learned predicate as a lookup table into a new Sieve_Learned.c, widening cacheObj.h:173's Sieve_obj_params_t from a bit to a few bits. Step 4: evaluate on held-out datasets and report the recovered fraction of the oracle gap against the metadata cost in Table 3's 17 B/object terms. LHD/lhd.cpp shows how a learned policy plugs into this codebase. Because perf_event_paranoid=3 blocks 'perf stat' on the target machine, substitute valgrind --tool=callgrind (pure user-space) for the instructions-per-request methodology of Fig. 11, and state the substitution.
addons.motivating_evidence: Paper section 6.2 / Fig. 12c: with foresight, 'SIEVE achieves the lowest miss ratio on 97% and 94% of the 1559 traces at the large and small cache size, respectively.' The authors explicitly frame this as 'the case that we have a perfect decision-maker choosing between the eviction candidates suggested by multiple simple eviction algorithms' and then stop - a large, explicitly measured, explicitly unexploited headroom, and the direct test of the paper's own 'SIEVE as a turn-key cache primitive' thesis (section 6.1). Section 7.1 supplies the counter-hypothesis to beat: 'When the cache size is large, most objects in the cache have few requests. Without enough features, a learned model can provide little benefits.'
addons.feasibility_rationale: Cross-cutting: needs a feature-logging build, an offline training pipeline that does not exist in the repo, a new eviction algorithm, and a train/test trace-split protocol to avoid overfitting. All CPU-only and all data is already staged locally, and in-tree LHD/GLCache/LRB demonstrate the integration pattern - but this is materially more than a localized patch, and the perf-to-callgrind substitution adds friction to the cost measurement.
addons.research_value_rationale: It converts a figure the paper only gestures at into a quantitative answer, and either outcome teaches something a reviewer at the original venue would want to know: if a 4-bit counter captures a third of the oracle gap, SIEVE's primitive thesis is vindicated at negligible cost and the ML-based policies (LRB, GLCache, LHD) look overbuilt; if it captures essentially nothing, that is concrete evidence for section 7.1's claim that eviction-time features are exhausted, which bears directly on the whole learned-caching line.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'learning-augmented cache eviction SIEVE Belady gap 2025'; 'arxiv 2025 cache eviction algorithm builds on SIEVE'; 'libCacheSim SIEVE variant 2025'. Closest: Learning-Augmented Heuristics / S4-FIFO (https://arxiv.org/html/2608.27975v1) shares the philosophy (simple heuristic on the data plane, learning off the critical path) and the simulator (libCacheSim), but tunes S3-FIFO's cache-level knobs from aggregate workload features, explicitly not object-level eviction decisions and explicitly not SIEVE, and never references the SIEVE-Belady headroom. SCION (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.01055) selects among unmodified policies using a 200k-request fingerprint. Neither targets the oracle gap inside SIEVE. Rated partial because reviewers will ask how this differs from S4-FIFO, and the proposal must answer that up front: object-level versus cache-level, oracle-gap-anchored versus knob-tuning.

addons.name: Reproducing SIEVE's scalability claim without CacheLib
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that a concurrent SIEVE built on a sharded hash table with a lock-free visited bit and a single lock taken only on the eviction path sustains at least 1.8x the throughput of a promotion-suppressing LRU at 16 threads on the Meta KV and Twitter traces, and that the resulting races on the hand pointer perturb the miss ratio by less than 0.1 percentage points relative to the serial simulator.
addons.mechanism: Build a standalone multi-threaded benchmark under example/, modelled on example/cacheSimulatorConcurrent/main.cpp - which today only parallelizes independent simulations via simulate_with_multi_caches (:56-58), not a shared cache, and therefore cannot answer this question. Make Sieve_obj_params_t::freq (cacheObj.h:173) an atomic byte written with a relaxed store on hit (Sieve.c:129), shard the chained hash table (dataStructure/hashtable/chainedHashTableV2.c), and take a single spinlock only inside Sieve_evict (Sieve.c:218-232). Baseline: an LRU (LRU.c) with CacheLib's 60-second promotion suppression described in section 4.3, implemented over the same sharded table so the comparison is apples-to-apples. Sweep 1/2/4/8/16 threads as in Fig. 6, and additionally report the miss-ratio delta against the serial cachesim run - a quantity the paper never measures.
addons.motivating_evidence: The abstract's scalability claim ('twice the throughput of an optimized 16-thread LRU implementation') and Fig. 6 rest entirely on a CacheLib prototype that is NOT in this repository - repo/README.md:67 points at the external Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23, and section 4.4 footnote 6 concedes that CacheLib's LRU optimizations make the SIEVE diff unquantifiable, which is why CacheLib is excluded from Table 2. Independent confirmation on a different substrate is therefore genuinely missing. Separately, the paper's core throughput argument - 'cache hits require no locking' (abstract) - is never paired with a measurement of what those unsynchronized hits cost in accuracy, even though several third-party lock-free SIEVE ports already ship on that assumption.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Needs a new harness and careful concurrent-code review; nothing in repo/ is thread-safe, so there is no starting point. It does fit the machine: 16 cores match the paper's thread count, and scaling to at most 4 GB of cache per thread (versus the paper's 4 x nthread GB, which would demand 64 GB at 16 threads on a shared 125 GB box with 111 GB free) keeps it safe. No root, no GPU, trivial compute. The risk is engineering time and correctness debugging, not resources.
addons.research_value_rationale: Making a headline result verifiable outside a 100-kLOC production library is real value, and the miss-ratio-under-races measurement is genuinely unmeasured and matters to anyone shipping SIEVE. Not H because the work is confirmatory rather than novel - the expected answer is 'the claim holds' - so only a surprising outcome (races materially hurting the miss ratio, or the LRU gap shrinking on a fair substrate) would move a reviewer.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'SIEVE lockfree concurrent cache implementation'; 'SIEVE scalability reproduction 2025'. Several independent lock-free SIEVE implementations exist - https://github.com/opencoff/go-sieve advertises 'lockfree, concurrent cache - faster and simpler than LRU', and there are further Go/Rust/Python ports - so the artifact itself is not novel. But none of them publish a controlled scalability-versus-optimized-LRU comparison or a miss-ratio-under-races measurement, which is the research content here. No academic follow-up found; CacheBench (https://ucsc-ospo.github.io/report/osre25/harvard/cachebench/2025-08-06-haochengxia/) re-evaluates miss ratios only, not throughput.

risks: 1492 of the 1559 traces (CDN1 and CDN2, paper Table 1) are proprietary and are not linked from repo/README.md:52-58, so the abstract's flagship statistic ('lower miss ratio than 9 algorithms on more than 45% of the 1559 traces') can never be reproduced as stated; only the 67-trace public subset is reachable and Fig. 3a/3b/3d/3e are permanently out of reach.

The scripts that actually draw the paper's figures are internal and broken: scripts/priv/plot/load_miss_ratio.py:15 imports a nonexistent module 'scripts.str_utils' (the file is at scripts/utils/str_utils.py) and plot_mr_red_box.py:265-266 hardcodes /disk/cphy/result/ while plotting algorithms (S3FIFO_delay-0.1000-2-0.50) that appear in no paper figure. Budget a day to rewrite aggregation against the stable output format at bin/cachesim/main.c:62-69.

Fig. 12a/b (ARC-SIEVE, TwoQ-SIEVE, LeCaR-SIEVE) is not reproducible from this repo at all: eviction/fifo/LP_ARC.c:110-120 is ARC-over-Clock ('LP-ARC-Clock'), and grepping every Sieve_init caller (QDLP.c:131, WTinyLFU.c:142, S3FIFOd.c:127, test/common.h:256, example/cacheSimulatorConcurrent/main.cpp:47) shows SIEVE is only composed into S3FIFO-style algorithms. A team wanting that result must implement it themselves.

Fig. 6 (throughput and scalability) requires an external artifact, Thesys-lab/cachelib-sosp23 - a fork of Meta's CacheLib with folly/fbthrift dependencies and a historically Docker-oriented build. Porting it to a rootless conda environment is a serious, unbounded risk; add-on A4 exists to route around it.

perf is unavailable on the target machine (perf_event_paranoid=3), so the instructions-per-request methodology of section 6.1 / Fig. 11 cannot be replicated directly. Substitute valgrind --tool=callgrind (user-space, no root) and disclose that the two tools count differently, so absolute numbers will not match.

Memory, not CPU, is the binding constraint: bin/cachesim/main.c:35 instantiates n_algo x n_size caches simultaneously via simulate_with_multi_caches, so naively running 11 algorithms x 2 sizes on Tencent (1038 M objects, 10% cache) would need hundreds of GB. The machine is also shared (111 GB available at measurement time, not guaranteed). Run algorithms serially and/or use --sample-ratio.

The fidelity of --sample-ratio is unverified: spatial object sampling (traceReader/sampling/spatial.c:33) is the cheapest scale-down, but neither the paper nor the repo documents how much it perturbs the relative RANKING of algorithms at a given cache size. Validate it on Meta CDN (small enough to run both sampled and unsampled) before trusting it on Tencent or Twitter.

No artifact-evaluation badge evidence could be obtained - the USENIX NSDI'24 presentation page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch and no badge markers appear in the repository - so there is no 'Results Reproduced' signal to lean on; treat badge status as unverified.

libCacheSim/ here is a frozen 2024-08-01 snapshot, not upstream 1a1a11a/libCacheSim, which has since diverged (e.g. a 3LCache directory exists upstream but not here). Develop against this snapshot for fidelity to the paper's numbers; rebasing onto upstream would silently change the baselines.

Scoop pressure is rising in the neighbourhood: CacheBench (UCSC/OSPO, 2025) is re-running 18+ algorithms including SIEVE over 8000+ traces on libCacheSim, and SCION and S4-FIFO both build learned components on libCacheSim. A pure re-evaluation of SIEVE is close to scooped; the four add-ons above are not, but the scoop check should be re-run at proposal time.
